title: Workflow: basics
summary: Work out Larkhaven Bikes fares with R: sums, values kept with `<-`, many values at once, comments and names, functions with named arguments, and what R's error messages tell you.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse)
steps.explain: `library(tidyverse)` attaches the core tidyverse packages. This lesson is mostly about R itself; its last step reads a file with readr's `read_csv()`.

steps.title: R as a calculator

runs.purpose: work out what a 20-minute ride costs a casual rider: $1.50 to unlock the bike, then 18 cents a minute
runs.task: Work out what a 20-minute ride costs a casual rider: 1.5 (the unlock fee) plus 0.18 (the price per minute) times 20.

runs.purpose: see what brackets change: add first, then multiply
runs.task: Put brackets around `1.5 + 0.18`, then multiply by 20, to see what brackets change.

steps.explain: R works a sum out in the order maths does, multiplying before adding, so `1.5 + 0.18 * 20` is {fare}: a 20-minute ride at a casual rider's fare on a classic bike. Brackets go first: `(1.5 + 0.18) * 20` is {bracketed}, which charges the unlock fee 20 times. The `[1]` in front of each answer marks its first value; a longer result shows the position of the first value on each line.

steps.title: Keep values: <- and the Environment

runs.task: Store 1.5 in a variable called `unlock_fee`. Type the arrow, `<-`, with Alt+- (Option+- on a Mac).

runs.purpose: keep the price per minute as `per_minute`
runs.task: Store 0.18 in a variable called `per_minute`, again typing `<-` with Alt+-.

runs.purpose: work out the 20-minute fare again, from the two names
runs.task: Work out the 20-minute fare again, using `unlock_fee` and `per_minute` instead of the numbers.

steps.explain: `<-` assigns: it keeps the value on its right under the name on its left. R prints nothing, but both names now appear in the Environment pane, each with its value. Alt+- types the arrow with a space each side. A name stands for its value, so `unlock_fee + per_minute * 20` gives {fare_again}, as before. When the fare changes, you change one line rather than every sum.

steps.title: Many values at once: c()

runs.purpose: keep the lengths of five trips, in minutes, in one vector, `minutes`
runs.task: Store the lengths of five trips, 12, 25, 8, 41 and 17 minutes, in a variable called `minutes`, with `c()`.

runs.purpose: work out what each of the five trips cost
runs.task: Work out what each of the five trips cost, from `unlock_fee`, `per_minute` and `minutes`.

steps.explain: `c()` combines values into a vector: {n_minutes} numbers under one name. Arithmetic on a vector works on every element. `per_minute * minutes` multiplies each length by 0.18, and the one unlock fee is added to each, so the answer has five costs: {costs}. The first, {first_cost}, is a 12-minute ride. R reuses the single unlock fee for every element; this is called recycling.

steps.title: Comments and names

runs.code: trip_cost <- unlock_fee + per_minute * minutes # what each trip cost
runs.purpose: keep the five costs as `trip_cost`, with a comment saying what it holds
runs.task: Store the five costs in a variable called `trip_cost`. After the code, add a comment: `#`, then what `trip_cost` holds.

runs.purpose: show `trip_cost`, mistyped with a capital T
runs.task: Type `Trip_cost`, with a capital T by mistake, and run it to see R's error.

steps.explain: R ignores everything on a line after `#`, so a comment is for people: use it to say what code is for, which the code itself can't. A name starts with a letter and holds letters, numbers, `_` and `.`; these lessons use snake_case, lower-case words joined by `_`, as in `trip_cost`. Names are case-sensitive and R doesn't guess what you meant, so it reports: object 'Trip_cost' not found. That message tells you where to look: the spelling and capitals of a name. The Environment pane lists the names that exist, and typing a name's first letters then pressing Tab completes it.

steps.title: Call functions: arguments by name

runs.purpose: list ride lengths from 5 to 60 minutes, in steps of 5
runs.task: List the numbers from 5 to 60 in steps of 5 with `seq()`, naming its arguments `from`, `to` and `by`.

runs.purpose: find the five trips' mean cost, rounded to the cent
runs.task: Find the mean of `trip_cost` with `mean()`, and round it to 2 decimal places with `round()` and its `digits` argument.

steps.explain: A function call is the function's name, then its arguments in brackets, separated by commas. `seq(from = 5, to = 60, by = 5)` names each argument and gives {n_seq} numbers. Given in order, arguments need no names: `seq(5, 60, 5)` gives the same, because `from`, `to` and `by` come first in `seq()`. Names make a call easier to read, and let you leave out arguments or give them in any order. One call can go inside another: `mean()` works out {raw_mean}, then `round()` rounds it to {mean_cost}. Typing `seq(` shows its arguments, and `?seq` opens its help page.

steps.title: Read an error message

runs.error: does not exist in current working directory
runs.purpose: read the fares table from `data/fare.csv`, with the file name mistyped
runs.task: Read `data/fare.csv` into `fares` with `read_csv()`. The real file is `fares.csv`, so read the error R gives.

runs.purpose: read the fares table into `fares`, with the file name right
runs.task: Fix the file name: read `data/fares.csv` into `fares`.

steps.explain: An error message says what went wrong, and often where. This one says there is no `data/fare.csv` in the working directory, the project's folder, which it names; the Files pane shows what is there. With the name right, `read_csv()` reads the table's {n_fares} rows into `fares` and reports the type it gave each column. The {n_current} rows whose `valid_to` is `NA` are today's fares, with no end date yet: a casual rider on a classic bike pays the 1.5 and 0.18 used above.
